F=ma Problem Series Lesson 1: 1D Kinematics
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:35:46 t V
Before we dive into the problems, a quick note:
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:35:48 t V
There are lots of little ideas for problem solving in this course. For example, today we'll learn about the harmonic mean, which is sometimes helpful in problems about speed. It's useful to know about the harmonic mean, but you can be a very good problem solver without having heard of it.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:36:16 t V
Also, I want to emphasize that this class is not designed for physics beginners.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:36:55 t V
Although, if you are a physics beginner you can still do a good job and learn a lot from this course. But you'll need a book!
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:37:21 t V
I'll put a couple of references on the message board as well.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:37:32 t V
We also want to practice some big ideas. Today's big idea is how to read key features on graphs. Key features are things like the minima and maxima, asymptotes, etc. We want to find those features and figure out what they mean in a particular physics problem. The meaning can change from problem to problem, so this is a hard skill. It's also a helpful skill in many different topics covered in this course and in physics we won't even cover here.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:37:48 t V
Our big ideas are usually strategies that are helpful throughout the F=ma exam, and often in all problem-solving.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:37:52 t V

Using and Interpreting Graphs
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:39:29 t V
While solving a kinematics problem, a student found the equation a=k−bv,a=k−bv, where aa is the acceleration of an object, vv is its velocity, and kk and bb are positive constants. Given that at t=0,v=0,t=0,v=0, which of the following vv vs tt graphs is consistent with the equation?
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:39:41 t V




jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:40:31 t V
Notice I've stickied the problem. You can also double click on anything I type, including graphs, and it will open in a window of its own.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:40:40 t V
(Another strategy: read the problem more than once, and read carefully! For instance, here, the word "positive" is very important. That's something to notice. It's harder to practice noticing the opposite, which is when that word isn't there!)
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:40:51 t V
A lot of people realize that a=k−bva=k−bv is an equation for a line, then choose (E). What's the problem with that?

jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:42:02 t V
Axis labels are important to read, too!
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:42:03 t V
The equation a=k−bva=k−bv is an equation for acceleration, a.a. It's in terms of velocity, v.v. So on an aa vs vv graph, that equation gives a straight line. The graphs given are all for vv vs t,t, though!
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:42:17 t V
We need a plan. It turns out to be fairly difficult to find the equation for v(t)v(t) (since it requires calculus).
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:42:40 t V
(I'll show you how on the message board - not that hard).
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:43:02 t V
Instead, let's figure out what the solution does. For example, we could find out whether v(t)v(t) always increases, or whether it oscillates up and down. We can do that without finding v(t)v(t) exactly.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:43:08 t V
Let's start with graph (A). Take a look at these two tt values.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:43:10 t V




jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:43:31 t V

position
velocity
acceleration
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:44:04 t V
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:44:09 t V
The velocity is the same at these two times. We can see this by comparing the height of the vv vs tt graph at the two points.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:44:22 t V




jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:44:27 t V
But the acceleration is different at the two times. We can see this because at the first time, the vv vs tt graph slopes upward, but at the second time it slopes downward.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:44:38 t V

jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:45:51 t V
No, it can't. If we know v,v, we can use the equation a=k−bva=k−bv to find a.a. If vv has the same value again later, aa will have the same value as well. And since aa is the slope of a vv vs tt graph, there can't be two places where vv is the same but the slope is different.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:46:26 t V
Is this clear?
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:46:56 t V
Notice that we're reasoning about graphs, but using an equation. We'll go from equation to graph and back again regularly in this course.

In (B), the graph flattens out. The acceleration gets closer and closer to zero, and the velocity gets closer and closer to some particular fixed value. This is called an asymptote.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:55:37 t V
The asymptote is when the graph flattens out, meaning aa approaches zero. If we set a=0a=0 in the equation, we get 0=k−bvt,0=k−bvt, where vtvt is the velocity at the asymptote.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 19:55:48 t V
Solving for vt,vt, vt=kb.vt=kb. This is the terminal velocity of the object.

Summary
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 21:01:52 t V
When looking at graphs, we can search for certain key features - where the zeroes, minima, and maxima are, and whether there's an asymptote.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 21:02:03 t V
By matching key features of a graph up to feature of an equation or of a physical scenario, we can determine which graphs fit with which mathematical or physical descriptions.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 21:02:18 t V
When an object is traveling at constant speed, its distance traveled, speed, and the time it travels are related by d=vt.d=vt.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 21:02:23 t V
We can't average (using the arithmetic mean) the speeds of objects traveling two equal distances at different speeds; that only works for objects traveling two equal times at different speeds.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 21:02:28 t V
Drawing a graph is often the easiest way to understand what's going on in a given problem.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 21:02:31 t V
Acceleration is the slope of a vv vs tt graph. Velocity is the slope of an xx vs tt graph.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 21:02:38 t V
Displacement (change in position) is the area under a vv vs tt graph. Change in velocity is the area under an aa vs tt graph.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 21:02:45 t V
In constant acceleration, the average speed is halfway between the initial and final speeds. This can be used to find the total distance traveled.
jonjoseph 2025-06-11 21:02:59 t V
Complicated-looking problems are usually easier when we adopt the right point of view. That could be drawing a graph, or it could be choosing the right reference frame.
